find: A state agency deploys a proprietary AI model to cut 75\% of in-home Medicaid nursing hours for low-income disabled adults after sending a generic notice citing ``updated clinical-risk scoring,'' offering a live ALJ hearing within 90 days. \textbf{Claimants' Case:} Means-tested medical care implicates \emph{Goldberg}-level subsistence risks, and ``black-box'' scoring destroys the transparent written contestability that saved the SSA process in \emph{Eldridge}. \textbf{``Opposite Side'' (State's Case):} Objective clinical data fits \emph{Eldridge}'s ``generality of cases,'' a 90-day hearing is far faster than \emph{Eldridge}'s one-year delay, and pre-termination hearings would drain scarce Medicaid funds. The case is close because the first factor points toward \textit{Goldberg} while the second and third can be argued either way: whether a generic notice of an algorithmic score lets claimants respond meaningfully before the cut is exactly the question \textit{Eldridge}'s reliance on detailed written notice leaves open.
replace: A state agency uses a model to propose substantial reductions in in-home Medicaid nursing hours. It gives each recipient the specific medical findings, explains the criteria used and the reasons for the proposed reduction, and lets the recipient submit a written response. A timely request for a hearing before the date of action maintains services where federal regulations require continuation. Some disputes turn on conflicting accounts of the help a recipient needs day to day. Under \textit{Mathews}, the State can argue that the individualized explanation, written response, and ability to maintain services reduce the risk of error. A recipient can argue that, when an assessment turns on credibility and live testimony could materially clarify it, those safeguards leave too great a risk of losing essential care. The constitutional question turns on those facts and the timing of any loss of services.
reason: Federal Medicaid rules require specific reasons and generally protect continuation if a beneficiary requests a hearing before the date of action, subject to exceptions. The original treats generic notice and a later hearing as a realistic legal baseline.
